opportunities.title: End-of-life of server-dependent software: live-service games
target_users: Demand side: players of shut-down server-dependent games (1,294,188 verified ECI signatories; Homecoming donors)
Action/payer side: publishers facing the EC end-of-life code of conduct (no demonstrated willingness)
opportunities.strongest_alternative: Community revival servers (Homecoming, Pretendo Network) plus commercial re-release of offline games (GOG Preservation Program, 337 games)
opportunities.strongest_counterevidence: The EC (16 Jun 2026) declined any legal obligation citing IP rights, and the parties who would have to act (publishers) show negative demand; even successful revivals cannot recover vendor-held account data (Pretendo: existing NNIDs do not work).
opportunities.falsifier: Sample 20 live-service games shut down 2024-2026 in EU/NA/JP; if >=50% already have an official offline mode or a working community server, the gap is small; if <10% do despite large communities, the blocker is legal, not technical.

demand.basis: Player demand demonstrated (ECI 1,294,188 confirmed by EC and heise; donations); publisher demand negative (EC reply, ESA); no evidence of demand for a new solution.

international.basis: Direct evidence in EU (ECI), NA (City of Heroes, VGHF) and Asia (Japan >70% live-service games end within 3 years); legal barriers differ by region.

innovation.basis: No checked alternative preserves server-side functionality, but community emulators partly cover the job; commercial sunsetting services not searched.

theme.basis: Specific discontinued games (City of Heroes) anchor the revived workflow.

ai.basis: AI may help protocol/server reconstruction, unevidenced in this session.

feasibility.basis: Needs a legally usable dead game with available client; licensing is the material risk.

demo.basis: Before/after (game refuses to start -> game playable) is clear to an international panel.

sustainability.basis: Homecoming monthly donation goals filled 'in days, if not hours' (PC Gamer, opened); paid re-release market exists (GOG); no evidence anyone pays for an EOL tool or standard.

changes.from: Community-run server emulators (Homecoming) plus voluntary publisher offline patches
changes.to: Community revival servers (Homecoming, Pretendo Network) plus commercial re-release of offline games (GOG Preservation Program, 337 games)

opportunities.title: Shutdown window of small/mid community platforms
target_users: Operators of small platforms that are closing (Cohost, Glitch)
opportunities.strongest_alternative: ArchiveTeam + Internet Archive + operator-built export/redirect + Mastodon-style documented exports (Activity Streams 2.0) + GDPR Art. 20
opportunities.strongest_counterevidence: Cohost and Glitch already shipped exports/redirects and ArchiveTeam archived Cohost; Cohost was small (21,142 MAU in Nov 2023), so the gap may be timing and funding rather than missing tools.
opportunities.falsifier: Review 20 platform shutdown notices from 2024-2026 (ArchiveTeam Deathwatch); if >=70% already provide export + redirect + >=90 days notice, the hypothesis fails.

demand.basis: Secondary evidence of shutdowns and archivist effort (R11-R14), Cyworld 2021 surge only as snippet; no direct demand for a new solution.

innovation.basis: ArchiveTeam, DTI and operator exports cover much of the job.

theme.basis: Specific shut-down platforms (Cohost, Glitch) but value is mostly archival.

feasibility.basis: Public exports/archives exist to work with; privacy limits scope.

sustainability.basis: Dying operators have no money (Cohost); Cyworld restoration failed for lack of funding.

opportunities.title: Unpreserved scholarly record (small and open-access journals)
opportunities.strongest_alternative: CLOCKSS / LOCKSS / Portico / PKP Preservation Network / Internet Archive Scholar (not opened this session)
opportunities.strongest_counterevidence: Part of the vanished journals may be predatory (Shelomi comment), and specialised preservation infrastructure already exists; the problem is participation, not technology.
opportunities.falsifier: Check 50 random 'unpreserved' DOIs from Eve's dataset; if >=80% are still accessible and captured by IA Scholar, urgency is overstated.

demand.basis: Peer-reviewed measurements (R5, R7) show the problem; no evidence of demand for a new solution.

international.basis: Laakso et al. report vanished journals across all regions; mechanism is global.

innovation.basis: Specialised archives already cover the core job.

theme.basis: No specific dead technology; fails the theme gate.

ai.basis: AI not needed for the core problem.

feasibility.basis: Open datasets exist; scope must be narrow.

sustainability.basis: Library membership models exist but were not verified this session.

changes.reason: C checked JASPER/PKP PN/Keepers (free incumbents) and read Eve more cautiously; C's evidence is stronger and B-O3 fails the theme gate
Single-study findings or author opinion; Eve reports 27.64% 'seemingly unpreserved'

opportunities.title: Heritage of dead regional platforms (Japanese keitai, early Chinese web, Mxit)
opportunities.strongest_alternative: Kahvibreak community tooling (ktdumper), DoJa 5.1 SDK emulator, SquirrelJME, Melange, G-MODE Archives re-releases; commercial re-releases (G-MODE Archives, HAMSTER Appli Archives)
opportunities.strongest_counterevidence: The bottleneck is hardware access and encryption keys, which the volunteer community is already solving; redistribution remains legally blocked.
opportunities.falsifier: Take the top 100 keitai games listed on Keitai Wiki; if >=70% are already dumped and run on existing emulators, there is no remaining software gap.

demand.basis: Large demonstrated volunteer effort (R8) but small community; no user demand for a new tool.

international.basis: Strong Asia evidence plus Africa (Mxit); NA/EU audience for keitai is unverified.

innovation.basis: Community tooling covers much of the job.

theme.basis: i-mode/EZweb are verifiably discontinued (services ended) and central to any demo.

ai.basis: Possible decompilation/translation help; not evidenced for keitai specifically.

feasibility.basis: Depends on dumped games and hardware not in hand; legal grey zone.

demo.basis: Lost game running again is visually clear.

sustainability.basis: Commercial re-release of keitai titles shows some paid demand for rescued content (Hit Save, single source); preservation tooling itself is donation-funded and legally grey.

opportunities.title: AI-assisted source reconstruction of abandoned software with a byte-match oracle
opportunities.strongest_alternative: m2c + decomp-permuter + objdiff community tooling; Ghidra/IDA; academic LLM-decompile models
opportunities.strongest_counterevidence: DecompileBench finds LLM decompilers 52.2% lower in functional correctness than commercial tools when no oracle is used, and the 74% match result comes from a single blog author on 60 functions. The tools-only (m2c + permuter) baseline is not published in text, so the LLM's marginal contribution is unmeasured.
opportunities.falsifier: Re-run a public matching-decompilation benchmark on 30 functions from a different project; if the LLM adds <15 percentage points over tools alone, AI is not load-bearing.

demand.basis: Decomp communities exist; demand not measured this session.

international.basis: Evidence only from one author and global open-source projects.

innovation.basis: Active area with academic and community entrants.

theme.basis: Abandoned software anchors the work but the dead technology is generic unless one title is chosen.

ai.basis: Byte-match oracle makes output mechanically checkable, but the only benchmark is a single blog (n=60) without a published tools-only baseline; load-bearing remains a hypothesis.

feasibility.basis: Needs a legally usable binary and an existing decomp project.

demo.basis: Function match is visible but needs explanation.

changes.reason: Coordinator AI-necessity check: conventional baseline not established
